KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

Showers with some thunder will tend to decrease in coverage
across the mountains of Maine and northern New Hampshire this
evening. These have been somewhat slow moving, with low 
environmental shear preventing these from sustaining an 
updraft. Other than some low stratus or fog development along
the coast and into the interior this evening, tonight should
remain fairly quiet.

Tuesday begins mostly dry as low pressure begins to close off 
arriving from the Great Lakes. The same low shear environment
will exist, but additional forcing and moisture will be arriving
across the western portion of the forecast area (New Hampshire
primarily). Hires guidance, including the HREF and REFS, has
continued to show the potential for isolated heavy rainfall
amounts greater than an inch across central and southern NH.
These are likely individual storms that can sustain themselves,
but are moving slow in limited flow magnitude. In a precip
efficient environment (PWAT greater than 1.25 inch, warm cloud
depth approaching 12kft, and mean RH greater than 90 percent)
the WPC's Marginal risk of excessive rainfall fits well for
isolated instances of flash flooding.

The caveat is this occuring over a portion of the forecast area
that has been very dry and has flash flood guidance values of 2
to 3.5 inch per one hour. If anything, the main concern may be
tracking areas that see decent rainfall Tuesday, ahead of the
more widespread rainfall into the remainder of the week.

Showers/thunder Tuesday should retreat west with the loss of
daytime heating, but can't rule out a few more showers rotating
in as the primary circulation pivots just to the west in NY.

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...
Global models are slowly coming into agreement on the evolution
of this weeks system, and one of those aspects is the surface 
low track. All camps now depict the center of the surface low, 
and for the most part the upper low, passing south of our area 
midweek. How exactly this impacts rainfall amounts seems to 
remain a point of contention, but one thing that can be said 
with confidence is that this will eliminate much of the 
influence from the low level jet. The spread in strength of the 
moisture transport has decreased with the ECMWF Ensemble, GEFS, 
and NAMNest all depicting PWAT values in the ballpark of 1.50 to
1.75 inches south of the mountains during the day Wednesday, 
with values 1.25 to 1.50 inches to the north. BUFKIT soundings 
also suggest warm cloud depths 10-12kft, so even without 
favorable jet dynamics rainfall is going to be efficient. That 
being said the difference in PWAT values is still causing some 
large spread in the modeled QPF. The Euro ensemble remains on 
the high end of the aforementioned range and maintains it's 
moderate to high confidence (50-70% probabilities) of a 
widespread 1-2 inch rainfall. Meanwhile, the GEFS is more in the
middle of the PWAT range and maintains its low confidence 
(10-30% probabilities) in rainfall exceeding an inch. This 
spread remains a forecast challenge, but I think at this point 
it is fair to say that Wednesday into Thursday is going to 
feature a more stratiform steady rain, and less in the way of 
convective features. Regardless, as mentioned earlier rain will 
be moderate to heavy at times and may pose an isolated urban and
complex terrain flooding threat. Elsewhere, recent dry 
conditions have left soils with high infiltration capacity and 
ample subsurface storage, which should absorb the bulk of 
initial rainfall. The exception would be locations that see 
heavy rainfall on Tuesday and are saturated going into the 
stratiform rain event. Bottom line: Confidence is increasing, 
albeit slowly, in a decent rain event Wednesday into Thurday, 
but confidence in amounts remains low and will hopefully be 
assisted by the CAMs as this event begins to shift into their 
window. Some showers linger through the day Friday, before 
tapering off in the evening.

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...
Global models are in surprisingly good agreement on the 500 mb 
pattern going into next week. Low pressure exits to the east on 
Saturday and a ridge builds making for a mostly dry day with 
temperatures in the low to mid-80s. Shower and thunderstorm 
chances return Sunday as a trough begins to approach, as usual 
its broad brush at this time range, but it likely won't be a 
washout. Monday may be a different story as all the models have 
an upper low somewhere in the vicinity, but of course it is to 
early to say for sure. Bottom line: We may only get a brief 
break in the wetter weather as the pattern looks to largely 
remain unsettled.
